A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QMC-slicing research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including v1 Appendix J becoming v2 Appendix K.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix J report original kernel-approximation and summation experiments, including convergence rates, runtime comparisons, and GPU evaluations.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix K retain the original experiments and add thin-plate-spline evaluations and an MMD gradient-flow experiment on CIFAR10.

M1.justification: Appendix I changes the rescaling constant from the maximum of the source and target radii to their sum, correcting the stated Fourier-summation preprocessing. The core slicing algorithm and distance-design optimization remain unchanged; this correction does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Appendix K.3 adds CIFAR10 in 3072 dimensions and an MMD gradient-flow task, extending evaluation from kernel approximation and summation to downstream optimization. Figure 8 also adds thin-plate-spline summation on Letters, MNIST, and FashionMNIST.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same RFF, ORF, Sobol RFF, slicing variants, and GPU PyKeOps comparisons. The new experiments reuse existing comparison methods; no comparator is added or removed from retained comparisons.

E3.justification: The new gradient-flow evaluation measures objective against runtime using 50000 target and generated particles, 1000 projections, and 50000 momentum-Euler steps with step size 1 and momentum 0.9. This introduces a substantial downstream evaluation protocol. Appendix I also revises the reported rescaling rule.

E4.justification: Appendix K.3 adds a case study testing whether improved kernel approximation translates into better optimization convergence. Existing kernel-width and dimensionality sensitivity analyses are retained from v1 Appendix J; the thin-plate-spline benchmark additions do not themselves constitute new ablations.

E5.justification: Retained approximation experiments still average 50 direction realizations and 1000 inputs, while summation comparisons retain 10 runs and standard-deviation shading. The added thin-plate-spline plots follow that practice. The gradient-flow experiment supplies no new seed, repeated-run, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 8 adds thin-plate-spline error-versus-time results, and Figure 11 adds downstream convergence results favoring QMC slicing. Remark 6 reports 0.2–0.3 seconds per slicing iteration and about one hour for exact PyKeOps gradient evaluation. Existing plotted results and numerical Tables 1 and 3–6 remain unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendix J introduces Proposition 5 and a proof comparing accuracy-dependent RFF and Fourier-slicing complexity under bounded-data and smoothness assumptions. Theorem 1(ii) also weakens the Riesz variance upper bound by dropping the subtraction of one from its coefficient. The new complexity derivation contains scaling inconsistencies.

C1.justification: After Corollary 4, v2 explicitly claims superior accuracy-dependent complexity over RFF for Gaussian summation, beyond v1's empirical comparisons and slicing-error guarantees. The introduction specifically emphasizes distance QMC designs; the abstract and conclusion otherwise retain their central claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly qualifies whether projected Sobol sequences satisfy the formal QMC-design definition. Appendix K.4 expands the explanation of the theory–experiment gap using effective dimension, symmetry, and hemisphere smoothness. Appendix K.3 also attributes improved flow convergence to more accurate gradients.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds access information for a general PyTorch slicing/NFFT implementation alongside the existing experiment code. Appendix K.3 supplies initialization, optimization parameters, hardware, and timing information for the new application, while Appendix I corrects the rescaling instructions.

R1.justification: New Appendix D.1 explicitly compares the bounds with Hertrich (2024), and related work distinguishes kernel slicing from sliced Wasserstein distances. Added citations support this discussion, the complexity analysis, and gradient flows. The Rux reference update identifies the same previously cited work.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with localized editing, more consistent distance-QMC terminology, and expanded explanations. Appendix D is subdivided, Appendix G gains RFF-summation background, and the new complexity appendix shifts the numerical appendix from J to K. Affiliation and publication-header text also change.

P2.justification: Figure 8 expands from three to six panels, and Figure 11 adds the gradient-flow plot. Figure 3 relocates, and surrounding material reflows. Existing plots and result-table structures remain intact, so the visual changes are localized additions.

improvement.justification: The added application, thin-plate-spline tests, qualifications, and implementation information improve empirical usefulness. However, the new complexity guarantee is not established as written: Proposition 5 states D proportional to epsilon^2|log epsilon| while its proof uses epsilon^-2|log epsilon|. Its Fourier-truncation parameter also fails to yield the claimed O(epsilon) bound when substituted into the displayed error estimate. These benefits coexist with a substantive new proof defect, preventing a confident net quality judgment.
